81.text: The Book of Intellect, Knowledge and Ignorance
Chapter 1: The merit of the intellect and the censure of ignorance

al-Baqara: "signs for a people who use their intellect"; and He, exalted, said: "thus does God make clear to you His signs, that perhaps you may understand"; and He, exalted, said: "yet none takes heed save those possessed of understanding."

Al 'Imran: "yet none takes heed save those possessed of understanding"; and He, exalted, said: "We have made clear to you the signs, if you would use your intellect"; and He said: "truly in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for those possessed of understanding."

al-Ma'ida: "that is because they are a people who do not use their intellect"; and He, exalted, said: "so fear God, O you possessed of understanding"; and He said: "and most of them do not use their intellect."
al-An'am: "but most of them are ignorant"; and He said: "and surely the abode of the hereafter is better for those who are godfearing — will you not then use your intellect?"
al-Anfal: "truly the worst of creatures in God's sight are the deaf and dumb who do not use their intellect."
Yunus: "can you then make the deaf hear, though they do not use their intellect?"; and He, exalted, said: "and He lays defilement upon those who do not use their intellect."
Hud: "but I see you are a people who are ignorant."
Yusuf: "truly We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, that perhaps you may understand."
al-Ra'd: "only those possessed of understanding take heed."
Ibrahim: "and that those possessed of understanding may take heed."
Ta Ha: "truly in that are signs for those possessed of reason."
al-Nur: "thus does God make clear to you the signs, that perhaps you may understand."
al-Zumar: "truly in that is a reminder for those possessed of understanding."

82.text: al-Mu'min: "a guidance and a reminder for those possessed of understanding"; and He, exalted, said: "and that perhaps you may understand."
al-Jathiya: "signs for a people who use their intellect."
al-Hujurat: "most of them do not use their intellect."
al-Hadid: "We have made clear to you the signs, that perhaps you may understand."

«1»- Ma'ani al-Akhbar; al-Amali of al-Saduq: al-Hafiz, from Ahmad b. 'Abd Allah al-Thaqafi, from 'Isa b. Muhammad al-Katib, from al-Mada'ini, from Ghiyath b. Ibrahim, from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, peace be upon him, who said: 'Ali b. Abi Talib, peace be upon them both, said: The intellects of women lie in their beauty, and the beauty of men lies in their intellects. (1)

Exposition: al-jamal (beauty) is excellence in form and in character. As for his saying, peace be upon him, "the intellects of women lie in their beauty" — the meaning may be that one ought not to look to their intellect, given its rarity, but rather be content with their beauty; or the meaning may be that their intellect is for the most part bound up with their beauty. The first is the more evident.

«2»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: al-'Attar, from his father, from Sahl, from Muhammad b. 'Isa, from al-Bazanti, from Jamil, from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said: The Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, used to say: The root of a man is his understanding, his intellect is his religion, and his manliness is where he places himself. The days are turns of fortune, and people are equal in their descent from Adam.

Exposition: al-lubb, with a damma on the lam, is the pure essence of anything, and also the intellect; the second is what is meant here. That is, the precedence of individual men in the nobility of their origin rests upon their intellects, not upon their lineages or their ancestral merits. Then he, peace be upon him, explained that the intellect which is the source of nobility appears only through choosing the true religion from among the religions, and through perfecting one's religion with the things that perfect faith. And al-muruwwa, with hamza and with a damma on the mim and the ra', is humanity (2), derived from al-mar' (man); it is sometimes lightened by substitution and assimilation. What is apparently meant is that a man's humanity, and his completeness or deficiency therein,

It may be that his intent, peace be upon him, was to urge men and encourage them toward what perfects their intellects, and to press them to abandon the adorning of their beauty and what pertains to their outward appearance. It is as when you say to a man: How much do you care for improving your appearance, the cleanliness of your face, the curling of your hair?! Leave that to women — a man's beauty lies only in perfecting his intellect and purifying his soul. On this reading, what is meant by "beauty" is excellence of outward form and of character.

He erred here, God have mercy on him, for derivations of this kind — insaniyya (humanity), muruwwa (manliness), futuwwa (chivalry) and the like — serve to convey the appearance of the effects of the root from which they derive. So the meaning of muruwwa is the appearance in a person of the qualities of the man (al-mar') as against the woman (al-mar'a): loftiness of outlook, overlooking petty faults rather than disputing them, fidelity, and the like.

83.text: …the lofty ranks and the base stations. How wide is the gap between one who is content for himself with nothing short of the full rank of knowledge, obedience, nearness and union, and one who is content to be a laughing-stock for base men for the sake of a meal or a morsel, and sees for himself no honour or standing beyond that.
It may also be that what is meant is marrying among one's equals, as
al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said to Dawud al-Karkhi when he wished to marry: Look where you are placing yourself.
But the general sense is the more evident.

Al-duwal — the dal taking any of the three vowels — is the plural of dawla, with damma or with fatha, both meaning the turning of time and the passing of wealth or of might from one person to another; with damma it also means victory in war. The meaning is that dominion over this world, its possession and its might belong one day to one people and another day to others. And "people are, with respect to Adam, shara'" — with the ra' unvowelled, though it is sometimes vowelled — that is, equal in lineage, all of them children of Adam. So these shifting, perishing things do not become the measure of nobility; rather nobility lies in the real and enduring things that last in both abodes. The last two clauses reinforce the first two.

«3»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: Ibn Idris, from his father, from Ibn Hashim, from Ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from Ibn Sinan (1), from al-Sadiq Ja'far b. Muhammad, peace be upon them both, who said: Five things — whoever lacks them has little in him from which benefit is drawn. It was said: And what are they, O son of the Messenger of God? He said: Religion, intellect, modesty, good character and good breeding. And five things — whoever lacks them, life is not pleasant for him: health, security, sufficiency, contentment, and a congenial companion.

«4»- al-Khisal: My father, from Sa'd, from Ibn Yazid, from Isma'il b. Qutayba al-Basri, from Abu Khalid al-'Ajami, from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him, who said: Five things — whoever lacks them has little in him from which benefit is drawn: religion, intellect, good breeding, freedom and good character.
al-Mahasin: Ibn Yazid, the like of it, except that it has "generosity" in place of "freedom".

Exposition: Good breeding (husn al-adab) is the conducting of one's affairs by the rule of the Sacred Law and of the intellect, in the service of the Truth and in dealing with created beings. And sufficiency (al-ghina) is to have no need of created beings — that is, sufficiency of soul, for that is the perfection, not

With a kasra on the unpointed sin and a fatha on the nun. It appears he is 'Abd Allah b. Sinan, who — as in the Rijal of al-Najashi — is Ibn Tarif, a client of the Banu Hashim, though it is also said a client of the Banu Abi Talib. He was treasurer to al-Mansur, al-Mahdi, al-Hadi and al-Rashid; a Kufan, trustworthy, one of our companions, of high standing, against whom nothing at all is impugned. He narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him. It has been said that he narrated from Abu al-Hasan Musa, peace be upon him, but that is not established, since Muhammad b. Sinan did not narrate from Abu 'Abd Allah, peace be upon him.

84.text: …sufficiency through wealth. As for "freedom", it may carry its apparent meaning, for it is a perfection in this world and its opposite is generally an obstacle to attaining the perfections of the hereafter; and it may be that what is meant by it is emancipation from bondage to the appetites of the soul and release from captivity to satanic whisperings. And God knows best.
«5»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: There is no beauty more adorning than the intellect.
He narrated it within a long sermon from the Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him; its full text will come in the chapter on his sermons, peace be upon him.

«6»- al-Amali of al-Saduq: Ibn Musa, from Muhammad b. Ya'qub, from 'Ali b. Muhammad b. 'Abd Allah, from Ibrahim b. Ishaq al-Ahmar, from Muhammad b. Sulayman, from his father, who said: I said to Abu 'Abd Allah al-Sadiq, peace be upon him: So-and-so, in his worship, his religion and his merit, is such and such. He said: How is his intellect? I said: I do not know. He said: Reward is according to the measure of the intellect. There was a man of the Children of Israel who used to worship God, mighty and exalted, on an island among the islands of the sea — green, verdant, thick with trees, with pure water. An angel among the angels passed by him and said: My Lord, show me the reward of this servant of Yours. So God, mighty and exalted, showed it to him, and the angel thought it little. Then God, mighty and exalted, revealed to him: Keep his company. So the angel came to him in the form of a man, and he said to him: Who are you? He said: I am a worshipping man; word of your place and your worship here reached us, so I have come to worship alongside you. He stayed with him that day, and when morning came the angel said to him: Your place here is truly a pleasant one. He said: Would that our Lord had a beast! If our Lord had a donkey we would pasture it in this spot, for this grass is going to waste. The angel said to him: But your Lord has no donkey. He said: Had He a donkey, grass such as this would not be going to waste. Then God, mighty and exalted, revealed to the angel: I reward him only according to the measure of his intellect. (1)

It may be said that what is meant by the reward is what is prepared for the weak and the simple-minded; or it may be said that reward follows upon the spirit of obedience and upon the servant's being compliant and obedient to his Master's command, just as punishment follows upon disobedience and upon his being in a posture of insolence and obstinacy. Since this worshipper was a believer, compliant toward God, exalted, reward follows upon his faith and his compliance even though he fell short in grasping some of God's attributes. And so you see that out of his love and compliance toward the Master he wishes the benefit to return to Him, glory be to Him, as is suggested by his words "Would that our Lord had a beast" and "If our Lord had a donkey we would pasture it" — all of this on the assumption that the report indicates his believing in corporeality. And it may be said that the soundness of a person's choices discloses the completeness of his intellect, and the absence of such soundness discloses its absence; so choosing the impossible when the possible could be chosen, or preferring the baser thing — pasturing his donkey — over the nobler, which is intimate discourse with God and worship of Him, discloses the deficiency of his intellect. On this reading the worshipper was not one who held God, glory be to Him, to be corporeal, as the phrase "if I were entrusted with it" suggests; but since his intellect was deficient, the full reward did not befit him.
